## TL;DR

I exercised Releases and Checks from the task worktree’s auth-less server using the existing preview fixtures in a headless Playwright browser. I covered release ready, pending auto-publish, and running states, plus the release cut drawer; for Checks I covered running progress, run timing history, reused checks, and navigation across all four tabs. At 1280 px and 375 px, the views I checked had no horizontal overflow, and the page console showed no errors. I found and fixed one action inconsistency: releasing a wedged local check slot used the browser’s native `confirm()` prompt. It now uses RepoOS’s shared confirmation dialog, with a test for cancel and confirm behavior. No real release was submitted.

## Work and rationale

The task asks for a user-oriented QA pass, so I started the worktree’s auth-less server with `just serve-noauth 7272` and drove its built app with Playwright Chromium. The computer-use browser host reported unavailable, but the locally installed Playwright package could connect to the server. This kept the inspection on the task branch without using or reading the main checkout.

On Releases I loaded `release:cutReady`, `release:autoPublishWaiting`, and `release:cutRunning`. The ready state showed the current and next versions and allowed the “Cut next release” action to open the cut drawer. I inspected its version, optional notes, and publishing explanation at both desktop and mobile widths, then stopped before its final action. The pending fixture showed the expected “Will publish” copy and Cancel control. The running fixture showed “RELEASING…” after its initial data load. Since this is a feature branch with an actual dirty working tree, its live release status also accurately explained that release cuts require main and a clean tree. I did not attempt to bypass those blockers. To cover terminal outcomes without invoking a release, I supplied mocked `/api/release/run` responses over the ready status fixture. The failed state showed its classified failure, failed tests, and output; the succeeded state showed the success outcome. Both fit at desktop and mobile widths.

On Checks I loaded the progress fixture on Now, then the timing and reuse fixtures on Runs. I clicked through Now, Runs, Test suite, and Check plan and confirmed that each tab selected correctly. The progress state displayed the current check and step count; the Runs fixtures displayed the completed row, timing summary, and reuse/skipped information. I also mocked the check-run list response with one failed and one passed completed run, expanded the failure row, and confirmed its failed-test detail appeared. I checked overflow at 1280 px and 375 px on each fixture page, mocked outcome, and the cut drawer; the document width matched the viewport in each observation. The browser console remained clear on the exercised routes.

The action review surfaced `window.confirm()` in `releaseWedgedSlot` in ChecksView. RepoOS’s UI conventions require designed dialogs for app actions, and a native prompt is inconsistent with the rest of this interface. I replaced it with the shared `ConfirmDialog`, which names the slot and managed process group/PID being terminated. Cancel closes the dialog without a request; confirmation sends the existing release request and refreshes local slot data. I added a test that proves both branches and checks the request count. This change preserves the existing endpoint and release semantics while making the user decision explicit in the application UI.

I documented the exercised fixtures, viewports, action, result, and fixture coverage limits in `docs/qa/2026-11-releases-checks.md`. In particular, the existing fixture set does not include a terminal failed or completed release cut. I did not invent those records or treat the release email failure fixture as proof of a failed release cut. Existing release tests cover the release completion and failure paths, but this browser pass does not claim visual coverage for those terminal cut states.

## Approaches tried

I first attempted to use the computer-use browser interface so I could inspect the running pages in the normal Chrome UI. That interface was unavailable in this environment. I then used the installed Playwright Chromium package against the same local auth-less server, exercising the fixture query strings, reading visible page text, checking browser console errors, checking `scrollWidth` against the viewport width, and taking temporary screenshots for visual inspection. Temporary scripts and screenshots were removed after the run.

For release actions, I opened the cut drawer but deliberately did not press the final Cut Next action. That tested the rendered path without tagging, pushing, publishing, or starting release work. For the Checks tab navigation I clicked each visible tab and checked both the selected-tab accessibility state and the current route query.

## Challenges and blockers

The `release:cutRunning` fixture pins a running run record while the release status is still read from the live server. The first short observation caught the page skeleton while that request was resolving; I waited for the page to settle before recording the running state. This is why the initial screenshot-like observation is not reported as a rendering defect.

The computer-use browser host being unavailable prevented interactive Chrome use. Local Playwright remained available, so it did not prevent testing the pages or interactions. The built-in preview fixture set does not pin every terminal state; Playwright route responses supplied those outcomes temporarily, without modifying server data or creating a release.

## Key learnings

The app can render useful release and check states from its existing `shotState` fixtures against a live worktree server, while still retaining real server blockers where the fixture does not intentionally pin status. Waiting for data to settle matters for the running-release view: its active run and its release readiness are separate pieces of state.

The remaining UI convention mismatch was easy to overlook because the wedged-slot action is an infrequent recovery operation. It is still a user-facing action with process termination consequences, so it benefits from the same clear, keyboard-accessible dialog behavior used elsewhere in RepoOS. The new test protects the important boundary: dismissing the prompt does nothing, while confirming makes one request.

The pass verified ready, blocked, running, failed, and succeeded release states, along with running progress and failed/passed completed run history in Checks. Separating the response state from the action under test made it possible to inspect failure and success presentations without performing a publish. The task handoff check remains the final verification for the branch.
